title: Prediction band with data (UQ propagation): how wide is the prediction uncertainty?
summary: When a model's parameters are uncertain, running it for many draws of the parameters gives a spread of predictions. The prediction band shows the median and the percentile ranges of that ensemble together with the data, so you can see whether the data fall inside the predicted uncertainty.

media.alt: Output against time for a damped oscillation: a teal median curve, a darker 68 percent band and a lighter 95 percent band around it that are widest near the first peak and the second hump, and twelve amber data points with small error bars lying within the bands.
media.caption: Reference render of class F8.3 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: How wide is the prediction uncertainty?
read_the_figure.axes: x: time in seconds (0 to 10). y: output in arbitrary units (about -0.9 to 1.2). Bands and median come from an ensemble of 400 parameter draws; data points carry plus or minus one standard deviation of noise.
look_at: Is the band definition stated (which percentiles) and how many ensemble members?
Where is the band narrow and where wide, and why (what is sensitive to the parameters)?
Do the data lie inside the bands, and about as often as the band's probability suggests?
Is the band the uncertainty of the model's parameters or of a new observation?
as_drawn: The legend defines the bands: 95 percent as the 2.5 to 97.5 percentile range and 68 percent as the 16 to 84 percentile range; the note says 400 parameter draws.
The median is a damped oscillation. The 95 percent band is about 0.6 wide at the first peak (about 0.85 plus or minus 0.3) and widest again near t = 7 to 8; it is narrowest near zero crossings.
Twelve data points with plus or minus one standard deviation noise bars (0.05) lie inside the bands; most lie inside the 68 percent band.
The outer edge of the 95 percent band is slightly wiggly, a sign that 400 draws estimate the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles only roughly.
read_the_figure.proves: If the data fall inside the band with about the stated frequency, the ensemble spread is consistent with what is observed. A band that excludes the data means that the model or its parameter distribution is wrong or that the noise is underestimated.
if_wrong: No band definition: 68 percent, 95 percent and plus or minus one standard deviation look alike but mean different things.
Data far outside the band: the model is biased or the uncertainty is too small.
A band mistaken for the range of a new measurement: a prediction interval would also include the measurement noise.
must_check: band definition stated: the percentile range is the meaning of the band, and without it the plot cannot be interpreted.

terms.meaning: A set of model runs with parameters drawn from their distribution.
The range between two percentiles of the ensemble at each time.
The probability that the band covers the true value if the ensemble is right: 68 percent or 95 percent.
Spread of predictions caused by not knowing the parameters exactly.
A band for a new observation: the ensemble spread plus the measurement noise.
The uncertainty of an estimated percentile because the ensemble is finite.

remember: 68 percent is the 16 to 84 percentile range, about plus or minus one sigma for a Gaussian.
95 percent is the 2.5 to 97.5 range, about plus or minus 1.96 sigma.
Prediction interval variance = ensemble variance + noise variance.
With N draws the 97.5th percentile has a standard error of about 0.13 sigma at N = 400.
State the band, the ensemble size and what the band represents.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position on x is time and on y the model output. The teal line is the median of the ensemble; two shades of teal give the 68 percent (darker, narrow) and 95 percent (lighter, wide) bands, nested so that more probable values are darker. Amber dots with small bars are the measured data and their noise. Colour distinguishes model (teal) from data (amber).

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: if you do not know exactly what the model's parameters are, you do not know exactly what it will predict. Running it many times with plausible parameters gives a cloud of curves, and the band is the cloud's envelope. Overlaying the data lets you ask the two questions that matter: is the data inside the cloud, and how big is the cloud compared with the question you want to answer?

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: The band reflects only the uncertainties that were put into the ensemble: if the model structure is wrong, a narrow band is confidently wrong. A band of the parameter ensemble is narrower than the range of a new observation, which also includes the noise. Percentiles of a skewed ensemble are not symmetric about the median, and a 16 to 84 band is only about one sigma for a Gaussian. The edges of the 95 percent band are noisy for 400 draws.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Draw a thin sample of individual ensemble curves ('spaghetti') to show correlation in time, which a band hides. A plot of the standardised residual (data minus median over band half-width) shows calibration directly. Report the fraction of data inside each band as a number.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add 20 individual ensemble curves in light grey, print the fraction of data inside each band in the legend, and add a dotted outer line for the prediction interval including measurement noise.

steps.title: Percentiles and sigma
steps.note: For a Gaussian ensemble the 16 to 84 percentile band is plus or minus one standard deviation (percentile points at -0.994 and +0.994 sigma for the exact 16 and 84 percent) and the 2.5 to 97.5 band is plus or minus 1.96.

steps.title: Prediction interval for a new observation
steps.note: At the first peak the ensemble sigma is about 0.16 and the noise is 0.05, so sigma_pred = 0.168: the noise adds little here, and would add much where the ensemble is narrow.

steps.title: How good is a percentile from N draws?
steps.note: For a standard normal, p = 0.975 and N = 400 this is 0.134 sigma, so the outer band wanders; use more draws for a smooth 95 percent band.

worked.title: Reading the prediction band of the reference render
worked.problem: (1) What are the width and the implied standard deviation of the ensemble at the first peak? (2) How many data points would you expect inside the 68 percent band, and how many inside the 95 percent band? (3) Is the band a prediction interval for a new measurement?

solution.text: (1) At the first peak the 95 percent band runs from about 0.55 to 1.17, about 0.62 wide, so half-width 0.31.

(2) For 12 points and a calibrated band: 68 percent of 12 is about 8 inside the narrow band and 95 percent is about 11 or 12 inside the wide band. The render shows all twelve inside the 95 percent band and most inside the 68 percent band: consistent.
(3) No: the band shows parameter uncertainty only. A prediction interval adds the noise variance.

worked.answer: Half-width 0.31 and sigma about 0.16; about 8 of 12 in the 68 percent band and 11 to 12 in the 95 percent band (observed: most and all); no, a prediction interval is slightly wider (0.168 against 0.16).

analyze.q: Why is the band narrow near the zero crossings and wide near the extrema?
analyze.hint: Which parameters change the amplitude and which the phase?

analyze.q: All twelve points are inside the 95 percent band. Is that good news?
analyze.hint: Expected number and the possibility of an over-wide band.

analyze.q: How would you check that the ensemble is too narrow?

evaluate.q: The data lie inside the band. Does it follow that the model is correct?
evaluate.hint: A wide band is easy to satisfy.

Compute the fraction of data inside each band and print it in the legend.

checks.q: What does the 68 percent band mean?
checks.answer: The range between the 16th and 84th percentiles of the ensemble at each time: if the ensemble is right, a new value falls in it 68 percent of the time.

checks.q: Ensemble sigma 0.2 and noise 0.1. What is the sigma of a prediction interval?
Only 4 of 12 data points fall in the 95 percent band. What are possible causes?
checks.answer: The model is biased or structurally wrong, the parameter distribution is too narrow, or the measurement noise is underestimated; a larger ensemble would not fix any of these.
